title: Emphatic Forms: A Debated Idea
short: Some forms put the stress on an adverb ("it was in the house that he heard"); scholars debate how many such forms exist and how to name them.
trouble: Students learn one theory as fact. Grammars differ here; this topic shows the main views and how to translate either way.

blocks.html: This lesson is different from the others. It does not teach a settled rule; it shows a question that Egyptologists have argued about for decades, and how to read texts while the argument goes on.

Some sentences seem to stress an adverbial part (a place, time, manner or purpose) rather than the verb: jj.n=j m njwt=j can be "I came from my town" or "it was from my town that I came". Scholars debate whether special emphatic verb forms mark this stress, how many there are, and what to call them.

Hieroglyphs hide vowels, and some verb forms that looked the same in writing probably sounded different. In Coptic, the last stage of the language, special "second tenses" put the stress on an adverbial phrase. H. J. Polotsky argued that Middle Egyptian had such forms too, among the sḏm=f and sḏm.n=f, and his view (often called the Standard Theory) shaped Egyptian grammar for a generation. Later scholars refined or challenged it. Some grammars, such as Allen's, speak of nominal forms; others prefer to describe stress through context alone. Gardiner's grammar of 1927 predates the debate and describes these forms in other terms.

rows: It was from my town that I came

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: In writing, a "plain" and an "emphatic" sḏm.n=f can look exactly alike; that is why the question is open.

items: The Standard Theory (after Polotsky): certain sḏm=f and sḏm.n=f forms are "emphatic" or "nominal"; they turn the verb into the background and make an adverbial part the real point of the sentence.
Revisions and critics: later work keeps some of the insight but questions how many separate forms exist, whether they are "emphatic" or simply nominal, and how far context alone explains the stress.
For the reader: most grammars agree that some sentences put the weight on an adverbial phrase, and that context is the best guide to when.

blocks.title: Two translations
blocks.q: Give a plain and an emphatic translation of jj.n=sn r sḏm mdt.
steps: Plain: "they came to hear the words".
Emphatic: the stress on the purpose, "it was to hear the words that they came".

blocks.html: Learning one theory as fact. A student who has read only one grammar may mark every other translation wrong. Grammars differ here, and good translators often give the plain version unless the context clearly calls for the stress (for example, when the sentence answers a question like "why did you come?"). Check: is the adverbial phrase the new information the passage is about? If so, an emphatic rendering may help; if not, the plain one is fine.

sources.name: H. J. Polotsky, Egyptian Tenses (Jerusalem, 1965), the "Standard Theory" of emphatic forms
James P. Allen, Middle Egyptian: An Introduction to the Language and Culture of Hieroglyphs (3rd ed., 2014), on the nominal forms of the sḏm=f and sḏm.n=f
